summary:
TerraPulse AI helps people investigate how environmental conditions change across places and over time. Built for NASA Space Apps’ “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” challenge, the prototype combines NASA POWER data with interactive maps, charts and statistical trend analysis.

Users can select a location, choose a supported variable such as air temperature or precipitation, and explore a historical record. They can compare locations, examine uncertainty and data coverage, and export findings.

TerraAgent, our Gemini-powered AI assistant, helps explain the selected analysis in everyday language. Users can ask about trends, compare periods and explore what statistical evidence means. Its explanations support understanding, while NASA data and the project’s calculations provide the evidence.

The interface shows sources, units, dates and limitations. Results represent NASA grid estimates near selected coordinates, and quality indicators are clearly distinguished from measurement accuracy.

Developed by Team Neurastra, TerraPulse remains a prototype. Future work includes testing more variables and locations, improving accessibility, and validating results against suitable station observations.
details:
TerraPulse AI helps people turn a question about environmental change into an investigation they can follow. Built by Team Neurastra for the “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” challenge, our prototype explores what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and how strong the statistical evidence is.

Users begin by selecting a place through the worldwide location picker, choosing a point on the map, or entering coordinates. They then select a supported environmental variable and time period. TerraPulse requests NASA POWER data for that location and presents the record through charts, trend estimates, uncertainty information and plain-language explanations. Additional tools support comparisons between locations, discovery of candidate trends, relationships between variables, and exports for further investigation.

NASA data is central to the project. We use NASA POWER’s public API to access meteorological, land-surface and radiation parameters. These include temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind and other supported variables. MERRA-2 provides the underlying meteorological reanalysis, while POWER’s radiation parameters draw on sources including CERES and GEWEX SRB. GeoNames supports place searches and coordinates, and Natural Earth provides geographic outlines for the maps.

TerraAgent adds a conversational way to explore the evidence. Powered by Google Gemini, it helps users ask questions about their selected analysis and understand technical concepts in simpler language. The environmental values come from NASA, and numerical calculations are performed by the analysis code. AI explanations should be checked against the displayed results and methodology.

We developed the interface with React, JavaScript, CSS, Vite and Recharts, supported by a Node.js backend and Vercel API functions. Python scripts help prepare and check stored data. Git and GitHub support version control and collaboration. Codex and Antigravity assisted with development, troubleshooting and documentation, with our team responsible for reviewing the work.

Our approach brings location selection, scientific analysis and explanation into one workflow. We want students, educators and curious users to explore environmental records while being able to trace each result back to its source.

Throughout development, we considered accessibility, mobile usability, free data access, incomplete records and scientific uncertainty. NASA POWER results describe grid estimates near selected coordinates; their resolution limits what can be concluded about an individual town. We also distinguish data completeness and reliability indicators from measurement accuracy. We have not independently validated every location against station observations.

TerraPulse AI remains a prototype. Our next steps include testing more locations and variables, improving the mobile experience, and comparing results with suitable station observations where available. Our intended impact is to make Earth system data easier to investigate and help users form thoughtful questions supported by evidence.
